title: Iran Sets a Two-Day Price for Hormuz, a Qatari LNG Carrier Is Hit in the Gulf, and Trump Says Ukraine Needs a New Leader Two Days Before the US Midterms
subhead: Istanbul's talks have not yet sat, but Iran has already named its terms for reopening the strait — sanctions relief, US force withdrawals and billions in frozen funds — while the election deadline in Washington is now hours away. Europe's youth protest wave turned violent in Frankfurt, and Bulgaria elected its first female president on a platform of dialogue with Moscow.

sections.heading: Tehran Puts a Two-Day Number on Hormuz
sections.body:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that talks with Qatari mediators had produced a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days of any agreement with Washington, shortened from an earlier five-day figure. He described the talks as ongoing and progressing but said no final conclusion had been reached (Al Jazeera interview, reported by Republic World and Reuters via CNA).

Araghchi also set out what Tehran wants in return: lifting sanctions imposed after the Islamabad memorandum, a reduction in US forces in the region, restoration of oil waivers, release of frozen Iranian funds including those held in Qatar, and recognition of the shipping routes Iran has discussed with Oman, with other routes closed (Republic World, citing Al Jazeera). His wording was that reopening the strait under those conditions would pave the way for negotiations on outstanding issues — meaning the corridor is being treated as an opening bid, not a settlement.

The negotiating format matters as much as the terms. Reuters reports Iranian negotiators in Doha on Sunday for a third consecutive day with Qatari mediators, with Qatar having shuttled to Tehran on Friday. President Trump has said the US will not strike before Tuesday's vote and has called the talks productive, but has not ruled out military action afterwards (CNA/Reuters).

In public, both sides are still building their case for the day after the vote. Trump said Saturday that the US has knocked out Iran's nuclear programme but still has 'one or two sites' to take care of and could do it 'in 10 minutes' (AFP, via Asharq Al-Awsat). Iran's army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia warned that a new war could last longer than the last one and that the American president would not set its duration; Defense Minister Mehrdad Akhlaghi promised a 'proportionate, decisive, and impactful' response; and IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said there would be no geographic limits to Iran's retaliation (Iranian state TV, via Asharq Al-Awsat and Xinhua).
sections.whyItMatters: The two-day window is a specific, testable offer for the first time. If it survives Tuesday, Washington faces a clear choice between a visible reopening of the world's most consequential oil chokepoint and a strike package it has already assembled.

sections.heading: Qatar's Own LNG Carrier Is Hit While Doha Mediates
sections.body:
Nakilat, Qatar's state-linked gas transport company, said the LNG carrier Al Mayeda was struck by 'unidentified objects' on Friday evening in the Gulf. No crew were injured and no environmental damage was reported; the vessel was described as safe and operational, with the impact still being assessed (statement published via the Qatar Stock Exchange, reported by Al Jazeera).

Qatar's foreign ministry condemned the attack as dangerous and a threat to maritime navigation and global energy supply security, said it reserved the right to take all necessary measures, and did not name a perpetrator (Qatar MFA on X, via Al Jazeera). Saudi Arabia expressed solidarity with Qatar, Bahrain called on the UN Security Council to act, and the GCC, the UAE and the internationally recognised Yemeni government also condemned it.

The scale behind the single incident is what gives it weight: more than 120 commercial ships have been hit in the region since the war began in February, according to International Maritime Organization and UK Maritime Trade Operations data. October was the worst month of the war for shipping, with at least 29 vessels struck (Al Jazeera). Iranian forces have said tankers passing without permission face 'destruction'; UKMTO separately reported a vessel struck in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday (Asharq Al-Awsat).
sections.whyItMatters: The mediator's own export fleet is now a target. That narrows Qatar's room to keep brokering on purely neutral ground, and it puts a Gulf state's sovereign assets directly on the retaliation list for whichever side is responsible.

sections.heading: Trump Tells Kyiv to Change Its President, and Kherson's Truce Ends
sections.body:
President Trump repeated his call for Ukraine to hold elections and suggested it get a new leader, blaming President Zelensky for a US deal to buy Russian diesel that reversed years of American sanctions on that trade (AP, BBC). The remarks landed as Ukraine's war effort is already being squeezed on the battlefield.

Zelensky said Russian strikes hit energy infrastructure in four regions overnight on Saturday, leaving hundreds of thousands of homes without power, with more than 60,000 still cut off in Dnipropetrovsk by evening. A separate strike killed two people, including a 13-year-old girl, in Vinnytsia region, according to the State Emergency Service. Ukraine struck a major missile fuel producer in Russia's Rostov region, damaging four production facilities, Zelensky said (BBC).

The rare humanitarian ceasefire that had allowed civilians to leave Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson region ended at 22:59 local time on Sunday. The pause, brokered with help from US First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo, had been expanded from Oleshky to the wider region. On Sunday evening Ukraine's air alert app was apparently hacked, with the air force having to publicly deny a false radiation warning for Kyiv (BBC).

Zelensky accused Moscow of exploiting Ukraine's shortage of ballistic missile interceptors and said Kyiv asks for Patriots from the US and Europe every day (BBC).
sections.whyItMatters: Public US pressure on Zelensky's legitimacy, delivered days before a summit track is due to reconvene, undercuts his position at the table. It also tells Moscow that Washington's patience is a variable it can work on while Ukraine's air defences thin out.

sections.heading: Frankfurt Burns, and Europe's Youth Protest Wave Turns Violent
sections.body:
Rioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as cost-of-living protests turned violent in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg. Police used water cannon against people attacking emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles; the windows of a gun shop were smashed and police seized two weapons after an arrest (BBC).

The demonstrations were organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt to protest school underfunding, the cost of living, public spending cuts and military service. Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported up to 18,000 protesters, roughly half the organisers' estimate. Hesse interior minister Roman Poseck said around 100 identified left-wing extremists had infiltrated the Frankfurt march. Berlin police reported 27 officers injured, and Hamburg police arrested 120 people (BBC).

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told Bild on Sunday that police had prevented 'violence like that seen in Paris' and called for harsh punishment of rioters (BBC). The German unrest came the same day as a third consecutive weekend of protests across France, with more than 320,000 demonstrators and over 770 arrests; in Paris, prosecutors opened an attempted murder investigation after petrol bombs were thrown at police, burning a gendarme's leg, with no arrest yet made for that attack (BBC, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez).

The underlying drivers are shared: cost of living, underfunded public services, and opposition to conscription. Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich told BBC the demonstrations were to 'fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion'.
sections.whyItMatters: Both countries are core NATO members now facing domestic resistance tied directly to defence spending and conscription. That is a political constraint on rearmament that will show up in budgets, not just in street clashes.

sections.heading: Bulgaria Elects Its First Woman President, and She Favours Talking to Moscow
sections.body:
Incumbent President Iliana Iotova won Sunday's runoff with between 57.4 and 58.2 percent against Andrey Gyurov, a banker and former caretaker prime minister backed by the pro-Western opposition, on 38.6 to 39.6 percent, according to estimates from several polling institutes (RTE, citing broadcasters). Iotova, 62, took over the presidency earlier this year when Rumen Radev stepped down to run for parliament, and is now the first elected woman president in the country of 6.4 million (RTE, AP).

Iotova favours dialogue with Moscow and opposes military aid to Ukraine, and governs alongside her ally Prime Minister Radev (RTE). Radev said the result showed the country had chosen 'the future over the past' — while also advocating dialogue with Moscow. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen congratulated her, citing security and defence, competitiveness and energy independence (von der Leyen on X, RTE). Gyurov accepted the results and called for unity.

The contest ran against the backdrop of suspected Russian interference: Radev's government has said attacks appeared to serve Russian interests and summoned the Russian ambassador, while conceding there was no direct evidence yet (RTE). Bulgarian Central Election Commission data reported by 24 Chasa showed Iotova ahead by a comparable margin with just over half of protocols counted.
sections.whyItMatters: Bulgaria sits on NATO's Black Sea flank and hosts the alliance's eastern air-policing rotations. A president who opposes arming Ukraine, elected outright, is a durable marker of how far Russian-aligned sentiment still reaches inside the EU's southeastern edge.

sections.heading: Beijing Makes Routine Patrols the Baseline East of Taiwan
sections.body:
Taiwan's Coast Guard said Beijing has no jurisdiction over waters around Taiwan, after China's coast guard claimed a flotilla led by the Hushi conducted 'routine law enforcement patrols' east of the island and said it had stepped up control of the surrounding waters. Taiwan said it shadowed two Chinese ships, the Hushi (CCG 1308) and Meishan (CCG 2303), with vessels including the Ji An, and accused Beijing of harassing ships through radio communications (CNA, Focus Taiwan).

The operational point is the shift from military signalling to administrative claim. Pai Pang-ting of Taiwan's Ocean Affairs Council told a security forum in Taipei that while the PLA provides high-visibility deterrence, Beijing uses coast guard, research and fishing vessels to challenge Taiwan's maritime law enforcement and administrative jurisdiction, and that it seeks to make repeated incursions look like routine management — gradually narrowing Taipei's ability to exercise jurisdiction over its own waters (CNA).
sections.whyItMatters: Coast guard presence creates a legal claim that grey-zone military exercises do not. Beijing is converting periodic pressure into a standing administrative fact on Taiwan's eastern approaches, the side that faces the Pacific and any external reinforcement.

sections.heading: Gaza: Eight Killed in a Year-Old Ceasefire, and the Peace Plan Stalls
sections.body:
Israeli strikes in Gaza killed at least eight people, including a four-year-old boy, despite a ceasefire that took effect in October last year. In Gaza City, a missile hit a group of civilians next to the Cairo School in Al-Rimal, killing three, including the child. In Khan Younis, a drone attack in Al-Mawasi killed five officers from the Hamas-run interior ministry, aged between 23 and 53 (BBC, hospitals and ministry officials).

The Israeli military said it struck military operatives in two attacks but has not provided evidence (BBC). Gaza's health ministry says 1,580 people have been killed since the ceasefire, and 74,594 since the war began; the UN considers its figures reliable (BBC). The Trump administration's peace plan for Gaza has stalled (BBC). In Sudan, the picture is a mirror image of unresolved war: around 30 countries plus the EU warned of an 'alarming deterioration' in food security and urged both warring parties to lift aid obstacles in a statement released by the State Department on Oct 26, while Britain sanctioned 15 SAF and RSF commanders over atrocities tied to the fall of El Fasher a year ago (US State Department statement, Reuters, Al Jazeera).
sections.whyItMatters: A ceasefire with a daily kill rate is not a ceasefire, and the stalled peace plan means no mechanism exists to change that. The same dynamic holds in Sudan, where the diplomatic track has stalled even as famine criteria sharpen.

bottomLine: The US-Iran war has produced its first concrete, time-bound offer: Qatar and Tehran have proposed reopening Hormuz two days after Washington accepts conditions that include sanctions relief, force reductions and released frozen assets — and that offer is being made while a Qatari LNG carrier is recovering from a strike and the IRGC promises retaliation with no geographic limits. The offer expires politically against Tuesday's midterms, after which Trump has explicitly kept one or two strike targets open. In Europe, the same day brought two signals of strain on the continent's security consensus: Frankfurt's riots over conscription and public spending, and Bulgaria electing a president who opposes arming Ukraine. Kyiv, meanwhile, is being asked by Washington to change its leadership while its power grid and air defences are being attrited.
